# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

---

## Compiler's Preface

I have undertaken this volume not as a work of criticism but as a work of custody. The letters collected here were written between 1984 and 2023 by Hideo Takashi, formerly of the Kenshikan school, latterly of the Enryō-ji monastery in Niigata Prefecture, and they were addressed, without exception, to me. I will not give my name. It is not relevant to the documents. I am the recipient and I am the compiler and I am, in whatever diminished capacity these roles imply, the editor. These designations are sufficient.

A brief account of the context may be useful.

On March 11, 1983, the All-Japan Invitational Championship final was held at the Nippon Budokan. The arena was filled to approximately two-thirds capacity. The referee was Ōnishi Genta, since retired. The bout was sanctioned at three points, full contact, with a five-minute regulation period and a two-minute extension in the event of a draw. Both fighters were announced. Both fighters approached the center line. The referee's hand dropped.

Hideo assumed his stance — left foot forward, weight distributed along the rear diagonal, hands positioned in what the Kenshikan school calls *tora no kamae*, the tiger's guard. He held this stance for between four and six seconds. Then he stepped back. He brought his feet together. He bowed once — not to me, not to the referee, but to the space between us, or perhaps to no one — and he turned and walked out of the gymnasium. The crowd produced a sound I have never been able to accurately describe. It was not booing. Neither was it silence. The referee consulted with the judges for eleven minutes. I was awarded the match by forfeit.

I did not see or speak with Hideo again.

Eleven months later — February 1984 — the first letter arrived at my home address in Ōsaka, which I had not given him and which at that time was unlisted. The envelope was standard: white, rectangular, bearing the monastery's return address in Hideo's hand, which I recognized from tournament registration documents. The postmark was stamped cleanly. The letter inside was folded with geometric precision, the creases so sharp they had nearly cut the paper. The stamp, however, was crooked — placed approximately fifteen degrees off the horizontal, its upper right corner lifting slightly from the envelope's surface as though it had been pressed down by a thumb rather than smoothed flat. I mention this because Hideo was, in every observable dimension of his life, a man of total physical exactitude. The crooked stamp was either an error he would not have made or a message I have never decoded.

I reproduce the envelope below, followed by the letter.

---

## Letter One

*February 3, 1984*
*Enryō-ji, Niigata*

The path from the gate to the main hall is two hundred and fourteen steps. I have counted them in rain and in dry weather and the number does not change, though the path feels longer when the cedar pollen falls in spring because one pauses to breathe and pausing interrupts the rhythm of counting. I note this because I have become interested in the difference between what can be measured and what can be experienced and whether these are, in the end, two descriptions of the same phenomenon or two phenomena that merely resemble each other.

I wake at half past three. We sit until five. We eat. We work. The work changes with the season — now it is clearing snow from the walkways, which collapses again by noon, which means the labor exists not to accomplish something but to teach the body that accomplishment is not the purpose of labor. I have some difficulty with this teaching. My body has been trained otherwise.

I wanted to tell you that I am here. I did not want you to wonder.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *The recipient's address, as stated in the preface, was unlisted at the time of this letter's arrival. Inquiries to the monastery's administrative office were not returned. Hideo's source for the address remains unknown.*

---

## Letter Two

*September 1984*
*Enryō-ji*

The maples along the northern ridge have begun their turn. There is a particular tree — I have no name for the variety; the abbot says it was planted before the monastery was rebuilt after the fire of 1889, which would make it at least a century old — whose leaves do not transition uniformly from green to red but instead produce, for a period of perhaps ten days, a mottling that contains both colors simultaneously, so that each leaf appears to be in argument with itself. The monks call this tree *Nidō-san* — "Mr. Two Minds." They find this amusing. I find it accurate.

The sitting practice continues. I am told that what I am doing is not yet sitting but merely the body's imitation of sitting, and that the difference will become apparent "when it does." This formulation is either profound or empty. I have not yet determined which, and I am told that this inability to determine is, itself, progress. I suspect the abbot is a more skilled opponent than anyone I met in competition, and his ring is one from which there is no walking away.

I use this metaphor reluctantly.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *The fire of 1889 destroyed the eastern wing of Enryō-ji. The monastery's records confirm a replanting program initiated in 1891 under Abbot Daisetsu. The specific maple Hideo describes has not been independently identified.*

---

## Letter Three

*June 1985*
*Enryō-ji*

Water. I have become preoccupied with water.

There is a stream that passes behind the meditation hall, narrow enough to step across in most seasons, which runs over a formation of granite that the monks have never attempted to clear or reshape. The water does not flow over the stone so much as it *negotiates* — finding the channels, pooling in the depressions, accelerating over the smooth faces, stalling against the rough ones. I have watched this stream for many hours across many months and I am unable to determine whether the water shapes the stone or the stone shapes the water or whether the question itself is the error of a mind trained to believe that every encounter must have an aggressor and a defender.

The granite is hard. The water is soft. The granite is still. The water moves. And yet the granite is the one that has been changed — hollowed, grooved, polished — while the water passes through apparently unaltered. But this is not true either, because the water that exits the stone formation is not the same water that entered it. It has been redirected. Its path has been permanently inflected by the encounter.

I am aware that I am not writing about water.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *No annotation necessary. The passage is self-evidently a meditation on hydrological processes as observed at the monastery site.*

---

## Letter Four

*January 1987*
*Enryō-ji*

I have not written in some time. The silence was not purposeful. Or — I will try to be more precise. The silence was purposeful at first and then it became habitual and then the habit became its own reason, and by the time I wished to write again I was unsure whether the wish was genuine or whether I was merely uncomfortable with the silence and wished to end my discomfort, which would mean the letter originated in weakness rather than in anything worth sending to another person. I sat with this question for several months. I have not resolved it. I am writing anyway.

The body remembers what the mind has agreed to forget.

This occurred to me during work practice last autumn. We were stacking firewood, a task that requires no thought, and I found my hands assuming a grip I had not used in years — the three-quarter hold, the one Sensei Morimoto taught for the heavy bag, with the smallest finger curled slightly beneath the others to stabilize the wrist. I was gripping a piece of oak the way I had been trained to grip a man's collar for a hip throw. My hands had not forgotten. They had merely been waiting for an object of approximately the right diameter and weight.

I wonder sometimes about the moral status of this kind of memory. The mind can renounce. The body cannot. It can only be redirected toward increasingly distant approximations of the thing it was trained to do, until the original purpose is buried under so many layers of substitution that it resembles something peaceful. But the structure remains. A fighting stance can become the posture of seated meditation if enough years pass. This does not mean the man has stopped fighting. It means the fight has moved inward, where there are no referees.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *The three-quarter grip described here corresponds to the modified* kumi-kata *taught at the Kenshikan school during the period 1975–1982 under Morimoto Yoshio (1929–2001). Hideo's description is technically precise. The grip was considered unorthodox and was the subject of some controversy at the 1981 regional qualifiers, where judges questioned its legality under then-current competition rules. It was ultimately permitted.*

---

## Letter Five

*November 1988*
*Enryō-ji*

When you and I trained — I will call it training, though perhaps we never trained together; perhaps we only competed, which is a different verb — there was a concept the Kenshikan instructors repeated so often it became invisible: *uke wo yobu*, "to call the receiver." The idea was that a stance is not merely a configuration of the body in preparation for action. A stance is an invitation. It presents certain openings — real or apparent — and in presenting them it asks the opponent to respond in particular ways. To adopt a fighting stance is therefore to begin a conversation in which you have chosen the first word and, if you are skilled enough, you have also constrained the possible second words to those for which you have a prepared reply.

But there is a depth to this principle that was never spoken of directly. A stance can contain an invitation the fighter has not consciously extended. The body, in assuming its trained configuration, may present openings the mind does not intend — asymmetries of weight, of tension, of micro-alignment — that speak to an attentive opponent below the level of strategy, below the level of language, in the grammar of the body itself. To read this grammar is a skill. To *speak* it unknowingly is a condition. And the distance between the two determines whether a match is a conversation or an interrogation.

I write this in the abstract because I am not yet prepared to write it any other way.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *The concept of* uke wo yobu *is not unique to the Kenshikan school. Variants appear in Yagyū Shinkage-ryū texts as early as the seventeenth century. Musashi addresses a related principle in the* Go Rin no Sho *(Book of Five Rings), Book of Water, under the heading "To Move the Shadow," which concerns provoking an opponent into revealing his intended technique. Hideo's extension of the concept — the uninvited opening, the body's involuntary speech — does not, to my knowledge, appear in any published martial text.*

---

## Letter Seven

*March 1990*
*Enryō-ji*

There is a bell in the western hall that cracked some forty years ago, before any of the current monks arrived except the abbot, who was then a novice. The crack runs vertically from the rim to approximately two-thirds of the bell's height and produces, when the bell is struck, a sound that is not a clean tone but a kind of shuddering — a fundamental note with a second, dissonant frequency vibrating against it, as though the bell is singing and wincing at the same time.

I asked the abbot why the bell has not been replaced. He told me that when the crack first appeared, a new bell was in fact commissioned, and that it arrived from the foundry in Kyoto six weeks later, and that when the monks rang it they found its tone "too pure." The new bell was sold to a temple in Hokkaidō. The cracked one remained.

A bell whose flaw has become its voice is not a broken bell. I am less certain about what it is. The abbot says: "It is the bell." He says this as though it resolves everything. Perhaps it does. The crack is not separate from the instrument. The dissonance is not a failure of the tone but the tone itself, the one this particular bell was always going to produce, even before the crack appeared — because the crack appeared because of some quality inherent in the metal, some brittleness or tension present from the moment of casting, which means the flaw was always there, which means the voice the bell has now is the voice it always had, only previously suppressed by the intact surface, which was — if I follow this thought to its end — the true distortion.

What I mean is: perhaps a thing is not most itself when it is whole.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *I have read this passage many times.*

---

## Letter Eight

*December 1991*
*Enryō-ji*

Winter again. I am writing shorter letters now because the cold makes my hand stiff and because I find that what I wish to say has become simpler, or else I have lost the ability to say the complicated things, or else the complicated things were never as complicated as my writing made them appear and what remains, after enough silence, is what was actually there.

I do not know why I write to you rather than to someone else or to no one. You have never replied. I have never expected you to reply. And yet the letters are addressed, and the address is not arbitrary, and this fact must mean something about the nature of what I am attempting to say, which is that it can only be said in a direction — not to the air, not to a journal, but to you, specifically, the one who was standing in front of me on that particular day, in that specific light.

I hope you are well. This is not a formality. I would like you to be well.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *Letter six has been omitted from this collection. It concerns exclusively administrative matters related to Hideo's formal renunciation of his competition ranking and his request to be removed from the All-Japan Martial Arts Federation registry. Its contents are of documentary interest only and do not contribute to the thematic architecture of the correspondence. The letter was dated August 1989. I have donated the original to the Federation's archive.*

---

## Letter Eleven

*October 1994*
*Enryō-ji*

Musashi writes of "the gaze in combat" — that one must look at the enemy's face with the eyes slightly narrowed, the attention wide, so that the whole body becomes visible without fixating on any part. He calls this *kanken*, "looking and seeing": to look at the broad field while seeing the specific threat. The principle is sound. But Musashi does not address the reverse condition: what happens when the specific thing you see is something the opponent does not know he is showing you.

A face in combat reveals everything. Not the emotions — those are controlled, or at least obscured, by anyone with sufficient training. What it reveals is *structural*. The tension in the jaw indicates where the breath is held. The direction of the lead eye indicates the intended angle of attack seven-tenths of a second before the body commits. The asymmetry of the brow — left side slightly higher than right, or the reverse — indicates which hemisphere of the brain is dominant in that instant: the left brow rises with spatial processing, the right with sequential reasoning, and a trained observer can determine from this alone whether the opponent is *planning* his next technique or *reacting* to yours.

I watched a great many faces in competition. I remember all of them. Most of them told me what the fighter was *going to do*. One face — only one — told me what the fighter *could not do*.

These are very different kinds of knowledge, and they carry very different obligations.

I had not intended to write this much. I will send it before I can reconsider.

Hideo

---

**Compiler's note:** *The passage on facial asymmetry and hemispheric dominance does not correspond to any published research known to me. I have consulted two neurologists, neither of whom could confirm or deny the claim. One described it as "plausible but unstudied." The other said: "This sounds like something a very particular kind of person would notice and no one else would ever think to look for."*

## Letter Fourteen

*June 1997*
*Enryō-ji*

A young monk arrived last month. He is perhaps twenty-three. He came from Tōkyō, from what he described as "a life of numbers" — banking, I believe, though he does not speak of it directly. He is eager in the way that young monks often are: mistaking rigor for progress. He sits with his spine so perfectly vertical that I can see the strain in his shoulders from across the hall.
